name: Indo-European spread
what: The family of English, Spanish, Russian, Persian and Hindi: about 3 billion native speakers, the largest on Earth.
why: Its spread is the best test case for whether languages move with farmers, with herders on horseback, or by elites; ancient DNA has reshaped the debate since 2015.

hypotheses.claim: Proto-Indo-European was spoken by herders on the Pontic-Caspian steppe around 4000 BCE and spread with Yamnaya and their descendants.
hypotheses.for: Shared words for wheels, wagons and wool point to after about 4000 BCE; steppe ancestry floods into Europe about 3000 to 2500 BCE and South Asia about 2000 to 1500 BCE.
hypotheses.against: Hittite Anatolia shows little steppe ancestry, so how Anatolian got there is unclear.

sources.cite: David W. Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (Princeton, 2007)
J. P. Mallory, In Search of the Indo-Europeans (1989)
Wolfgang Haak et al., "Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe", Nature 522 (2015)
Will Chang, Chundra Cathcart, David Hall and Andrew Garrett, "Ancestry-constrained phylogenetic analysis supports the Indo-European steppe hypothesis", Language 91 (2015)

hypotheses.claim: Indo-European spread out of Anatolia with the first farmers from about 7000 BCE.
hypotheses.for: Some Bayesian language trees date the root to 7000 to 6000 BCE and place it in Anatolia.
hypotheses.against: Wheel and wagon vocabulary is shared across branches and wheels are invented about 3500 BCE; ancient DNA shows the big turnover in Europe at 3000 BCE, not with farmers.

sources.cite: Colin Renfrew, Archaeology and Language: The Puzzle of Indo-European Origins (1987)
Remco Bouckaert et al., "Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family", Science 337 (2012)

hypotheses.claim: The deepest ancestor was spoken south of the Caucasus; one branch went to Anatolia, another north to the steppe and became Yamnaya, the source of most other branches.
hypotheses.for: Yamnaya carry ancestry from the Caucasus-Armenia region; this explains why Anatolian split first without steppe genes.
hypotheses.against: Still a reconstruction from genes and dated trees; no inscriptions survive from that time.

sources.cite: Iosif Lazaridis et al., "The genetic history of the Southern Arc: a bridge between West Asia and Europe", Science 377 (2022)
Paul Heggarty et al., "Language trees with sampled ancestors support a hybrid model for the origin of Indo-European languages", Science 381 (2023)

stages.name: Altai (Afanasievo)
stages.note: Steppe herders reach the Altai; often linked to the ancestors of Tocharian.

stages.name: Danube and Carpathian basin
stages.note: Yamnaya burials appear on the Hungarian plain.

stages.name: Central Europe (Corded Ware)
stages.note: Corded Ware people carry about three quarters steppe ancestry.

stages.name: Britain (Bell Beaker)
stages.note: Beaker-associated people replace about 90% of Britain's gene pool.

stages.name: Southern Urals (Sintashta)
stages.note: Chariots and fortified towns; ancestors of the Indo-Iranians.

stages.name: Kanesh, Anatolia
stages.note: First written Indo-European words (Hittite names in Assyrian merchant tablets).

stages.name: Punjab (Indo-Aryan)
stages.note: Rigvedic Sanskrit composed; steppe ancestry arrives in South Asia.

stages.name: Hallstatt (Celtic)
stages.note: Celtic languages spread across Iron Age Europe.

stages.name: Iranian plateau
stages.note: Old Persian is the language of the Achaemenid empire.

stages.name: The Americas
stages.note: Spanish, Portuguese, English and French spread with conquest and settlement.

sources.cite: David W. Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (Princeton, 2007)
J. P. Mallory, In Search of the Indo-Europeans (1989)
Wolfgang Haak et al., "Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe", Nature 522 (2015)
Will Chang, Chundra Cathcart, David Hall and Andrew Garrett, "Ancestry-constrained phylogenetic analysis supports the Indo-European steppe hypothesis", Language 91 (2015)
Colin Renfrew, Archaeology and Language: The Puzzle of Indo-European Origins (1987)
Remco Bouckaert et al., "Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family", Science 337 (2012)

name: Austronesian spread
what: About 1,270 languages from Madagascar to Easter Island, including Malay, Tagalog, Malagasy, Maori and Hawaiian.
why: Before 1500 it covered more of the globe than any other family, carried by outrigger canoes.

hypotheses.claim: Proto-Austronesian was spoken in Taiwan about 5,000 years ago; nine of the ten top branches are only on Taiwan.
hypotheses.for: Taiwan holds almost all the deep diversity; dated language trees show pulses and pauses that match the archaeology.
hypotheses.against: Some argue for an Island Southeast Asian origin with Taiwan as one source.

sources.cite: Robert Blust, The Austronesian Languages (revised ed., 2013)
Peter Bellwood, First Migrants: Ancient Migration in Global Perspective (2013)
Russell Gray, Alexei Drummond and Simon Greenhill, "Language phylogenies reveal expansion pulses and pauses in Pacific settlement", Science 323 (2009)

stages.name: Mariana Islands
stages.note: A long open-sea crossing into Micronesia.

stages.name: Bismarck Archipelago (Lapita)
stages.note: Lapita pottery marks the jump into the Pacific.

stages.name: Madagascar
stages.note: Speakers from southeast Borneo reach Madagascar; Malagasy is closest to Ma'anyan.

stages.name: Society Islands
stages.note: East Polynesia settled late and fast.

stages.name: New Zealand
stages.note: The last big landmass settled by humans.

sources.cite: Robert Blust, The Austronesian Languages (revised ed., 2013)
Peter Bellwood, First Migrants: Ancient Migration in Global Perspective (2013)
Russell Gray, Alexei Drummond and Simon Greenhill, "Language phylogenies reveal expansion pulses and pauses in Pacific settlement", Science 323 (2009)

name: Bantu spread
what: About 500 Bantu languages, including Swahili, Zulu, Shona and Kikongo, are a single branch of Atlantic-Congo.
why: One of the largest farming-language expansions; it reshaped the genes and languages of half a continent.

hypotheses.view: Grassfields origin, through and around the rainforest
hypotheses.claim: Bantu began near the Nigeria-Cameroon border and spread south and east over 3,000 years.
hypotheses.for: Closest relatives of Bantu are spoken there; language trees and genomes put the root there.
hypotheses.against: Whether the eastern branch split early (north of the forest) or late (after crossing it) is debated; genetics favours a late split.

sources.cite: Jan Vansina, "New linguistic evidence and the Bantu expansion", Journal of African History 36 (1995)
Rebecca Grollemund et al., "Bantu expansion shows that habitat alters the route and pace of human dispersals", PNAS 112 (2015)
Etienne Patin et al., "Dispersals and genetic adaptation of Bantu-speaking populations in Africa and North America", Science 356 (2017)

stages.name: Western rainforest
stages.note: Farmers move along rivers and savanna corridors.

stages.name: Great Lakes (Urewe)
stages.note: Iron working spreads with Eastern Bantu.

stages.name: Zambia and Malawi
stages.note: Foragers there are later replaced almost entirely.

stages.name: Limpopo, South Africa
stages.note: Early Iron Age farmers reach the far south.

sources.cite: Jan Vansina, "New linguistic evidence and the Bantu expansion", Journal of African History 36 (1995)
Rebecca Grollemund et al., "Bantu expansion shows that habitat alters the route and pace of human dispersals", PNAS 112 (2015)
Etienne Patin et al., "Dispersals and genetic adaptation of Bantu-speaking populations in Africa and North America", Science 356 (2017)

name: Afroasiatic spread
what: Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic, Somali, Hausa, Berber and dead Egyptian, Akkadian and Phoenician.
why: The family of the first written languages (Egyptian and Akkadian) and of the Bible and the Quran.

hypotheses.claim: Afroasiatic began among foragers in northeast Africa; five of its six branches are only in Africa.
hypotheses.for: Branch diversity is highest in Africa; Semitic looks like a branch that left.
hypotheses.against: Too old for comparative dating to be firm.

sources.cite: Christopher Ehret, Reconstructing Proto-Afroasiatic (Proto-Afrasian) (1995)

hypotheses.claim: It began with the first farmers of the Levant and spread into Africa.
hypotheses.for: Some shared words look agricultural.
hypotheses.against: The farming words are disputed, and African branch diversity argues the other way.

sources.cite: Alexander Militarev, "The prehistory of a dispersal: the Proto-Afrasian (Afroasiatic) farming lexicon", in Examining the Farming/Language Dispersal Hypothesis (2002)
Igor Diakonoff, Afrasian Languages (1988)

stages.name: Akkad, Mesopotamia
stages.note: Akkadian is written; it slowly replaces Sumerian.

stages.name: Ethiopian highlands
stages.note: Semitic arrives from South Arabia; later Ge'ez and Amharic.

stages.name: North Africa and Iberia
stages.note: Arabic spreads with the conquests, over Berber, Coptic and Aramaic.

sources.cite: Christopher Ehret, Reconstructing Proto-Afroasiatic (Proto-Afrasian) (1995)
Alexander Militarev, "The prehistory of a dispersal: the Proto-Afrasian (Afroasiatic) farming lexicon", in Examining the Farming/Language Dispersal Hypothesis (2002)
Igor Diakonoff, Afrasian Languages (1988)

name: Sino-Tibetan spread
what: Chinese, Tibetan, Burmese and about 500 more, spoken by about 1.4 billion people.
why: The second-largest family by speakers; its spread is tied to millet farming on the Yellow River.

hypotheses.claim: Proto-Sino-Tibetan was spoken by Yellow River millet farmers (Yangshao, Majiayao) about 6000 to 5000 BCE.
hypotheses.for: Two independent dated trees (2019) both put it in north China in the Neolithic.
hypotheses.against: Dates differ by over a thousand years between the studies.

sources.cite: Laurent Sagart et al., "Dated language phylogenies shed light on the ancestry of Sino-Tibetan", PNAS 116 (2019)
Menghan Zhang, Shi Yan, Wuyun Pan and Li Jin, "Phylogenetic evidence for Sino-Tibetan origin in northern China in the Late Neolithic", Nature 569 (2019)

hypotheses.claim: The family began in the eastern Himalayas or Sichuan, where diversity is highest.
hypotheses.for: Many small, very different branches in the Himalayas.
hypotheses.against: Diversity can build up in mountains long after a spread.

sources.cite: George van Driem, Languages of the Himalayas (2001)

stages.name: Eastern Tibetan plateau
stages.note: Tibeto-Burman speakers move west and south.

stages.name: Anyang
stages.note: Old Chinese written on oracle bones.

stages.name: Yangtze and the south
stages.note: Chinese spreads south over Tai, Hmong-Mien and Austroasiatic speakers.

sources.cite: Laurent Sagart et al., "Dated language phylogenies shed light on the ancestry of Sino-Tibetan", PNAS 116 (2019)
Menghan Zhang, Shi Yan, Wuyun Pan and Li Jin, "Phylogenetic evidence for Sino-Tibetan origin in northern China in the Late Neolithic", Nature 569 (2019)
George van Driem, Languages of the Himalayas (2001)

name: Uralic spread
what: Finnish, Estonian, Hungarian, the Sámi languages and many in Russia.
why: Hungarian sits in the middle of Europe 3,000 km from its relatives; ancient DNA links the spread to a Siberian ancestry.

hypotheses.claim: Proto-Uralic was spoken around the Volga-Kama about 2500 to 2000 BCE.
hypotheses.for: Loanwords from early Indo-Iranian fix it near the steppe edge; dated trees agree.
hypotheses.against: Others place it east of the Urals in western Siberia.

sources.cite: Riho Grünthal et al., "Drastic demographic events triggered the Uralic spread", Diachronica 39 (2022)

hypotheses.claim: The homeland was east of the Urals.
hypotheses.for: A Siberian-related ancestry spreads west with Uralic speakers.
hypotheses.against: Tree-word evidence fits both sides of the Urals.

sources.cite: Thiseas Lamnidis et al., "Ancient Fennoscandian genomes reveal origin and spread of Siberian ancestry in Europe", Nature Communications 9 (2018)

stages.name: Kola and Fennoscandia
stages.note: Siberian ancestry reaches the far north (Bolshoy Oleni Ostrov).

sources.cite: Riho Grünthal et al., "Drastic demographic events triggered the Uralic spread", Diachronica 39 (2022)
Thiseas Lamnidis et al., "Ancient Fennoscandian genomes reveal origin and spread of Siberian ancestry in Europe", Nature Communications 9 (2018)

name: Turkic spread
what: Turkish, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kazakh, Uyghur, Tatar and Yakut.
why: Spread mostly by conquest and nomad confederations, from Mongolia to the Balkans in 1,500 years.

hypotheses.claim: Proto-Turkic split up around 2,100 years ago in Mongolia and southern Siberia.
hypotheses.for: The oldest Turkic texts (Orkhon, 732 CE) are there; a dated tree gives about 2,100 years.
hypotheses.against: Whether the Xiongnu elite spoke Turkic is unknown.

sources.cite: Alexander Savelyev and Martine Robbeets, "Bayesian phylolinguistics infers the internal structure and the time-depth of the Turkic language family", Journal of Language Evolution 5 (2020)
Peter Golden, An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples (1992)

stages.name: Central Asia
stages.note: Oghuz and Karluk Turks; Iranian languages retreat.

stages.name: Anatolia
stages.note: After Manzikert, Turkish spreads over Greek and Armenian.

sources.cite: Alexander Savelyev and Martine Robbeets, "Bayesian phylolinguistics infers the internal structure and the time-depth of the Turkic language family", Journal of Language Evolution 5 (2020)
Peter Golden, An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples (1992)

name: Dravidian spread
what: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Brahui: about 250 million speakers.
why: Whether the Indus civilisation spoke Dravidian is one of the big open questions of history.

hypotheses.claim: Proto-Dravidian was spoken in peninsular India about 4,500 years ago.
hypotheses.for: Dated tree; old farming words fit Southern Neolithic crops.
hypotheses.against: Brahui in Pakistan is far from the rest.

sources.cite: Vishnupriya Kolipakam et al., "A Bayesian phylogenetic study of the Dravidian language family", Royal Society Open Science 5 (2018)
Bhadriraju Krishnamurti, The Dravidian Languages (2003)

hypotheses.claim: The Harappans spoke an early Dravidian language, pushed south later.
hypotheses.for: Brahui survives in the northwest; Indus signs read as Dravidian by some.
hypotheses.against: The Indus script is undeciphered, so this cannot be tested.

sources.cite: Asko Parpola, The Roots of Hinduism: The Early Aryans and the Indus Civilization (2015)
Vishnupriya Kolipakam et al., "A Bayesian phylogenetic study of the Dravidian language family", Royal Society Open Science 5 (2018)
Bhadriraju Krishnamurti, The Dravidian Languages (2003)
Asko Parpola, The Roots of Hinduism: The Early Aryans and the Indus Civilization (2015)

name: Austroasiatic spread
what: Vietnamese, Khmer, Mon and the Munda languages of India.
why: Probably the language of the first rice farmers of mainland Southeast Asia.

hypotheses.view: Middle Mekong / southern China rice farmers
hypotheses.claim: Austroasiatic spread with farmers from southern China into Southeast Asia around 2500 to 2000 BCE.
hypotheses.for: Neolithic farmers at Man Bac in Vietnam carry East Asian ancestry also found in Austroasiatic speakers.
hypotheses.against: Its homeland is still argued between the Yangtze, Mekong and northeast India.

sources.cite: Paul Sidwell and Roger Blench, "The Austroasiatic Urheimat: the Southeastern Riverine Hypothesis", in Dynamics of Human Diversity (2011)
Mark Lipson et al., "Ancient genomes document multiple waves of migration in Southeast Asian prehistory", Science 361 (2018)
Hugh McColl et al., "The prehistoric peopling of Southeast Asia", Science 361 (2018)

stages.name: Eastern India
stages.note: Munda speakers mix with local South Asians.

sources.cite: Paul Sidwell and Roger Blench, "The Austroasiatic Urheimat: the Southeastern Riverine Hypothesis", in Dynamics of Human Diversity (2011)
Mark Lipson et al., "Ancient genomes document multiple waves of migration in Southeast Asian prehistory", Science 361 (2018)
Hugh McColl et al., "The prehistoric peopling of Southeast Asia", Science 361 (2018)

name: Tai-Kadai spread
why: Thai and Lao reached their present homelands only about a thousand years ago.

hypotheses.claim: Southwestern Tai left the Guangxi-Guizhou border area between about 700 and 1000 CE.
hypotheses.for: Layers of Chinese loanwords date the split.
hypotheses.against: The deeper family date is uncertain.

sources.cite: Pittayawat Pittayaporn, "Layers of Chinese loanwords in Proto-Southwestern Tai as evidence for the dating of the spread of Southwestern Tai", MANUSYA 20 (2014)

stages.name: Sukhothai
stages.note: A Thai kingdom in the Chao Phraya basin.

sources.cite: Pittayawat Pittayaporn, "Layers of Chinese loanwords in Proto-Southwestern Tai as evidence for the dating of the spread of Southwestern Tai", MANUSYA 20 (2014)

name: Uto-Aztecan spread
what: Nahuatl, Hopi, Comanche, Shoshone and about 60 more, from Idaho to El Salvador.
why: Nahuatl was the language of the Aztec empire; the family's direction of spread is a famous dispute.

hypotheses.claim: Uto-Aztecan began in the north as foragers and moved south.
hypotheses.for: Northern branches lack old maize words.
hypotheses.against: Requires farming to be borrowed late.

sources.cite: William Merrill, "The historical linguistics of Uto-Aztecan agriculture", Anthropological Linguistics 54 (2012)
Lyle Campbell, American Indian Languages: The Historical Linguistics of Native America (1997)

hypotheses.claim: Maize farmers in west Mexico spread the family north into the Southwest.
hypotheses.for: Maize vocabulary reconstructs for the whole family.
hypotheses.against: The reconstruction is disputed.

sources.cite: Jane Hill, "Proto-Uto-Aztecan: a community of cultivators in central Mexico?", American Anthropologist 103 (2001)

stages.name: West Mexico
stages.note: Nahuan speakers move toward central Mexico.

stages.name: Tenochtitlan
stages.note: The Mexica found their capital; Nahuatl becomes the empire's language.

sources.cite: William Merrill, "The historical linguistics of Uto-Aztecan agriculture", Anthropological Linguistics 54 (2012)
Lyle Campbell, American Indian Languages: The Historical Linguistics of Native America (1997)
Jane Hill, "Proto-Uto-Aztecan: a community of cultivators in central Mexico?", American Anthropologist 103 (2001)

name: Quechua spread
what: Quechua, spoken by about 8 million people in the Andes.
why: It was spread by states (Wari, then the Inca, then Spanish missionaries), not by farmers moving into empty land.

hypotheses.claim: Proto-Quechua was spoken in central Peru; Inca Cuzco got Quechua late.
hypotheses.for: The deepest branch (Quechua I) is in central Peru.
hypotheses.against: Dates are loose.

sources.cite: Rodolfo Cerrón-Palomino, Lingüística aimara (2000) and Lingüística quechua (2nd ed., 2003)
Paul Heggarty and David Beresford-Jones, "Agriculture and language dispersals: limitations, refinements, and an Andean exception?", Current Anthropology 51 (2010)

stages.name: Cuzco (Inca)
stages.note: Inca make Quechua the language of empire.

stages.name: Bolivia and Ecuador
stages.note: Spanish missions use Quechua as a lingua franca.

sources.cite: Rodolfo Cerrón-Palomino, Lingüística aimara (2000) and Lingüística quechua (2nd ed., 2003)
Paul Heggarty and David Beresford-Jones, "Agriculture and language dispersals: limitations, refinements, and an Andean exception?", Current Anthropology 51 (2010)

name: Pama-Nyungan spread
what: About 300 languages covering nine tenths of Australia.
why: A recent spread over a continent people had lived in for 50,000 years.

hypotheses.claim: Pama-Nyungan began near the Gulf of Carpentaria about 5,700 years ago and spread south and west.
hypotheses.for: A dated tree of 306 languages.
hypotheses.against: Why it spread (no farming) is unexplained.

sources.cite: Remco Bouckaert, Claire Bowern and Quentin Atkinson, "The origin and expansion of Pama-Nyungan languages across Australia", Nature Ecology & Evolution 2 (2018)
Remco Bouckaert, Claire Bowern and Quentin Atkinson, "The origin and expansion of Pama-Nyungan languages across Australia", Nature Ecology & Evolution 2 (2018)

name: Inuit (Thule) spread
what: Inuit languages from Alaska to Greenland are almost the same because they spread so recently.
why: The Thule replaced the Paleo-Eskimo (Dorset) people of the eastern Arctic.

hypotheses.claim: Thule Inuit left north Alaska about 1200 CE and reached Greenland within a century.
hypotheses.for: Radiocarbon dates and genomes.

sources.cite: T. Max Friesen and Charles Arnold, "The timing of the Thule migration: new dates from the western Canadian Arctic", American Antiquity 73 (2008)

name: Athabaskan spread
what: Navajo and Apache in the Southwest are related to languages of interior Alaska and Canada.
why: A 3,000 km move south shortly before Europeans arrived.

hypotheses.claim: Athabaskan spread from Alaska; Apachean speakers reached the Southwest about 1400 CE.
hypotheses.for: Eyak and Tlingit, the closest relatives, are in Alaska.
hypotheses.against: The link to Siberian Yeniseian (Dene-Yeniseian) is proposed but not accepted by all.

sources.cite: Lyle Campbell, American Indian Languages: The Historical Linguistics of Native America (1997)

name: Arawakan spread
what: Taíno, Wayuu, Asháninka and dozens more across South America and the Caribbean.
why: The language of the people Columbus met.

hypotheses.claim: Arawakan spread from western Amazonia along rivers, with farming villages.
hypotheses.for: Branch diversity.
hypotheses.against: Dates rough.

sources.cite: Michael Heckenberger, "Rethinking the Arawakan diaspora", in Comparative Arawakan Histories (2002)

stages.name: Puerto Rico
stages.note: Ceramic Age settlers move into the Caribbean.

sources.cite: Michael Heckenberger, "Rethinking the Arawakan diaspora", in Comparative Arawakan Histories (2002)

name: Tupian spread
what: Guarani (official in Paraguay) and Old Tupi, the coastal lingua franca of colonial Brazil.
why: Tupi-Guarani had spread along the whole Atlantic coast by 1500.

hypotheses.claim: Tupian began in Rondônia, where most branches are.
hypotheses.for: Branch diversity.

sources.cite: Aryon Rodrigues, "As consoantes do Proto-Tupí" and Rodrigues and Cabral, Tupian (2012), in The Indigenous Languages of South America

name: Japonic spread
why: Japanese arrived with rice farmers from Korea; the Ainu are descendants of the earlier Jomon.

hypotheses.view: Korean peninsula with Yayoi rice farmers
hypotheses.claim: Proto-Japonic came to Kyushu with Yayoi farmers about 900 BCE.
hypotheses.for: Japonic place names in old Korean records; genomes show a Yayoi influx.
hypotheses.against: The wider Transeurasian family (with Turkic, Mongolic, Korean) is rejected by most linguists.

name: Mongolic spread
what: Mongolian, Buryat, Kalmyk; Khitan is an extinct relative.
why: Spread across Eurasia with the Mongol empire, but stayed only where Mongols settled.

hypotheses.claim: Proto-Mongolic was spoken in eastern Mongolia around 1000 CE.
hypotheses.for: The Khitan were the nearest known relatives.

sources.cite: Juha Janhunen (ed.), The Mongolic Languages (2003)
Juha Janhunen (ed.), The Mongolic Languages (2003)
